lling on a hard, smooth surface the s a portion of the tire flattened out: <math>p_1</math> and <math>p_2</math> are the intensities of the pressures at points <math>a_1</math> and <math>a_2</math> at equal distances in front of and behind <math>c</math>, the geometrical point of contact: <math>p_1</math> opposes, <math>p_2</math> assists the rolling of the wheel. At usual speeds the opposing force, <math>p_1</math>, will be greater than the force of restitution, <math>p_2</math>, the difference being a measure of the elastic hysteresis of the material, <math>H</math>, at that speed. If the vertical compression <math>cd</math> of the tire be denoted by <math>y</math>, the energy lost may be said to be proportional to <math>Hy</math>. Comparing three tires of steel, solid rubber and air respectively rolling on a smooth, hard surface, <math>H</math> is probably smallest for steel and largest for rubber, <math>y</math> is least for steel, greater for a pneumatic tire pumped is therefore <math>W/p</math>. Fig. 4 shows the shapes of the areas of contact of a bicycle tire 28 in. by 1½ in., for various amounts of vertical flattening, the figures annexed to the curves in plan and to the corresponding lines in elevation indicating the amount of vertical flattening in sixteenth parts of an inch. Let <math>y</math> be the vertical flattening, <math>a</math> the semi-major axis, and <math>b</math> the semi-minor axis of the curve of contact. For small values of <math>y</math>, corresponding to a tire pumped hard, the curves of contact may be considered plane sections of a circular ring. The area of the curve may be taken equal to that of an ellipse having the same axes, ''i.e.'' <math>\pi ab</math>. But
{{block center|<math>a = \sqrt{R^2 - (R-y)^2} = \sqrt{2Ry - y^2} = \sqrt{y}\, \sqrt{2R-y},</math>}}
{{block center|and <math>b = \sqrt{r^2 - (r-y)^2} = \sqrt{y}\, \sqrt{2r-y},</math>}}
<math>R</math> and <math>r</math> being the principal radii of section of the tire longitudinally and transversely. Therefore, approximately,
{{block center|<math>A = \pi ab = \pi y \sqrt{2R-y} \sqrt{2r-y}.</math>}}
For small values of <math>y</math>, <math>y</math> may be neglected in comparison with <math>2R</math> and <math>2r</math> respectively, and the above equation becomes
{{block center|<math>A = 2\pi y \sqrt{Rr} = \pi y \sqrt{Dd},</math>}}
{{block center|and therefore <math>W = 2\pi yp \sqrt{Rr} = \pi yp \sqrt{Dd}.</math>}}

For larger values of <math>y</math>, <math>A</math> is smaller than that given by the above formula, as shown in fig. 5, which gives the areas of contact plotted with respect to the vertical flattenings for a tire 28 in. by 1½ in. The same curve may serve to show values of <math>W</math>, thus corresponding to the load-deflection curve of a spring. The curve clearly shows the small value of the pneumatic tire as a spring device. Thus, when pumped hard, so that the normal load is carried with ⅛ in. vertical flattening, when the bicycle is travelling quickly, a lump on the road equivalent to ⅛ in. further flattening nearly doubles the upward reaction on the wheel. With the normal load carried with ⅜ in. vertical flattening the same lump on the road increases the upward reaction by only 23%, the area of contact of the tire being increased from 6·5 to 8 sq. in. The above brief investigation, involving a few approximations, is yet sufficiently accurate to afford a clear idea of the usual conditions of a tire.
